He explained that, while traveling from home through Datchet, he had been surprised to see smoke rising from the inn’s chimney. Hoping to find people there who could join him on the journey, he knocked and was let in. Only Lucy and her mother remained. Rheumatism had left her mother unable to move her limbs, and one by one everyone else in the district had departed, leaving the two women alone. Lucy begged the man to stay. In a week or two, she said, her mother would improve and they could leave together. Without help, abandoned like this, they would die. The man replied that his wife and children were already with the emigrants, which to his mind made staying impossible. As a last resort, Lucy gave him a letter for Idris, asking him to deliver it wherever he might find us. At least he carried out that task, and Idris was deeply moved as she received the following letter:

“Honored Lady,

“I am certain you will remember me and feel sorry for me, and I dare to hope you will help. What other hope do I have? Please forgive the way I write; I am so confused. A month ago, my dear mother lost the use of her limbs. She is improving already, and in another month I am sure she could travel in the way you so kindly offered to arrange. But now everyone has left—everyone. As each person went, they said perhaps my mother would recover before we were entirely abandoned. Three days ago I visited Samuel Woods, who had stayed until the last because of his newborn child. There were so many in his family that I thought I might persuade them to wait a little longer for us. But their house was empty. I saw no one after that until this good man arrived. What will happen to us? My mother does not know our situation. She is so ill that I have kept it from her.

“Please send someone to help us. I am sure we will die miserably if we remain as we are. If I tried to move my mother now, she would die on the road. And when she improves, even if I could somehow find the roads and make my way all those many miles to the sea, you would all be in France. That great ocean, frightening even to sailors, would lie between us.

“These were the events that tormented Felix and made him, when I first saw him, the most unhappy member of his family. He could have borne poverty, and since it had been the reward for his honorable actions, he took pride in it. But the Turkish merchant’s ingratitude and the loss of his beloved Safie were more bitter misfortunes, seemingly beyond repair. The Arabian woman’s arrival now breathed new life into him.

“When word reached Leghorn that Felix had lost his fortune and social position, the merchant ordered his daughter to forget her lover and prepare to return to her native country. Safie’s generous spirit rebelled against the command. She tried to reason with her father, but he left in anger, repeating his tyrannical demand.

“A few days later, the Turk came into his daughter’s room and hurriedly told her that he believed someone had revealed his whereabouts in Leghorn. He feared he would soon be handed over to the French government. He had therefore hired a ship to take him to Constantinople and would sail within hours. He intended to leave his daughter with a trusted servant. She could follow in her own time with most of his property, which had not yet reached Leghorn.

“Once alone, Safie considered what she should do in this crisis. She found the thought of living in Turkey unbearable; both her religion and her feelings opposed it. Some of her father’s papers came into her possession, and from them she learned of her lover’s exile and the name of the place where he was living. For a while she hesitated, but eventually she made her decision. Taking some jewels of her own and a sum of money, she left Italy for Germany with an attendant, a native of Leghorn who understood the language commonly spoken in Turkey.

“She safely reached a town about twenty leagues from De Lacey’s cottage. There her attendant became dangerously ill. Safie cared for her with the greatest devotion, but the poor young woman died. The Arabian was left alone, unable to speak the country’s language and entirely unfamiliar with the ways of the world. Fortunately, she found herself among kind people. The Italian attendant had mentioned their destination, and after her death the woman in whose house they had stayed made sure Safie reached her lover’s cottage safely.”

She was right concerning the rats. Every little while one poked his nose from a hole in the corner. She said that when she was by herself she had to keep things close by to throw, or they wouldn’t leave her in peace. She showed me a lead bar bent into a knot and said she could generally aim it pretty well, but she’d strained her arm a day or two before and wasn’t sure she could throw straight now. She watched her opportunity, though, and presently let fly at a rat. She missed by a good distance and cried “Ouch!” because it pained her arm so much. Then she said I should try the next one. I wanted to clear out before her old man returned, but naturally I didn’t show it. I took the lead, and the first rat to put out his nose got a throw from me. If he’d stayed put he’d have been a mighty sick rat. She called it first-rate and thought I’d catch the next. She fetched the lump back, bringing a hank of yarn for me to help with. I raised both hands, and she slipped the hank over them and kept talking about her husband’s affairs and her own. Then she stopped to say:

“Watch out for the rats. Best keep the lead in your lap where you can reach it.”

Just then she dropped the lump into my lap. I snapped my legs together over it, and she continued talking—but only for a minute or so. Then she lifted off the yarn, looked pleasantly and straight into my face, and said:

“Now, come on, what’s your proper name?”

“Wh—what, ma’am?”

“Your real name. Is it Bill, or Tom, or Bob—or what?”

I expect I trembled like a leaf, hardly knowing what to do. But I said:

“Please don’t make fun of a poor girl, ma’am. If I’m troubling you here, I’ll—”

“No, you won’t. Sit still and stay right there. I’m not going to harm you, or tell on you either. Tell me your secret and trust me with it. I’ll keep it safe, and help you besides. My old man will too, if you need him. You’re just an apprentice that’s run away, that’s what it is. It’s nothing to worry about. There’s no harm in it. Somebody’s treated you badly, and you decided to leave. Bless you, child, I’d never give you away.
